title: Burnings on both sides
hook: Mary burned Protestants; Elizabeth executed Catholics; both called it faithfulness

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thomas More: the king's good servant, but God's first. Your line was god's first.

In the middle of a street in Oxford, a small cross is set into the road. It's easy to walk over it without looking down. It marks the place where Protestants were burned, Cranmer among them. In London, near where the old Tyburn gallows stood, Catholics keep the memory of priests and laypeople who were hanged there. Two places. Two sets of the dead. The same country. Each side honored its own martyrs, and each side had killed the other's.

Under Queen Mary, England went back to Rome, and Protestants who would not return were tried for heresy and burned. Hugh Latimer and Nicholas Ridley, both bishops, were burned together at Oxford. John Foxe reports that Latimer told his friend to be of good comfort and play the man, because together they would light such a candle in England as, he trusted, would never be put out. Then Mary died, and her sister Elizabeth, the daughter of Anne Boleyn, became queen. The prayer book came back. Now Catholic priests, trained abroad, slipped into England in secret to say Mass in private houses. The law called them traitors. Priests were hanged, drawn and quartered, and people who sheltered them could die too. In York, Margaret Clitherow, a butcher's wife who hid priests in her home, was pressed to death. Edmund Campion, a Jesuit priest, was executed at Tyburn, and accounts say he prayed for the queen who had condemned him. Both sides called it faithfulness. Mary's courts saw heresy as a poison that could kill souls forever. Elizabeth's courts saw a priest from Rome as a threat to the crown. Each side was sure it was protecting something holy, and each was reading the same Gospel, where Jesus says, in the King James Bible: "By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." Christians on each side still honor their own martyrs. Some have begun to remember the other side's martyrs too, and to say two words the story leaves behind: never again.

Think of people on the other side of a line that matters to you, in politics, faith, family or an old quarrel, and do what the two sets of martyrs never got from each other: name one thing they hold dear, something they'd hate to lose. No need to agree or excuse anything; just wish them good: safety, rest, the thing they love kept safe. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, hold them kindly a while.
Latimer. The bishop burned with Nicholas Ridley under Queen Mary, who told his friend they would light a candle in England that would never be put out.
Your line: never again. Two sets of the dead, one Gospel. Day eight hundred seventy-one, done.

howItsDone: Anglicans and other Protestants remember those burned under Mary, often through Foxe's Book of Martyrs, while Catholics honor the English and Welsh martyrs of Elizabeth's reign as saints; some churches now hold services that remember both together.

chat.says: In England back then, were only Catholics punishing Protestants for their faith?
options: Both: Queen Mary burned Protestants, and Queen Elizabeth had Catholic priests killed.
Yes, the Protestant rulers who came after Mary never put a single person to death.
No, it was really only Protestants punishing Catholics, all the way through.

notes: Editor pass: swapped Matthew 5:44 (quoted on day 862) for John 13:35 and updated screen, match pair, fork reveal and practice to match; Latimer paraphrase now keeps Foxe's 'I trust'; removed 'a short ride away' (Oxford to London is not short) and the claim that people walk over the cross every day.
Claims rule: no dates or counts of the dead are given for either side.
Latimer's words to Ridley are paraphrased from Foxe ('be of good comfort, Master Ridley, and play the man; we shall this day light such a candle...'); attributed to Foxe.

Oxford: the cross set in the road in Broad Street marks the place of the burnings of Latimer, Ridley and Cranmer; confirm. Tyburn: Catholics remember martyrs near the site (e.g. the Tyburn convent shrine); confirm wording.
Margaret Clitherow pressed to death at York for harboring priests; Edmund Campion's prayer for the queen at Tyburn is attributed to 'accounts'. Confirm both.
'Some, today, have begun to remember the other side's martyrs too' and howItsDone 'some churches now hold services that remember both': general; confirm or soften.
Both sides presented without ranking; Anglican and Catholic Keepers should each confirm the balance.
